deep.reconstruction:
CONTEXT (my interpretation). The two printed formulas describe the projection of an inclined Kepler orbit onto a reference plane: rho is the projected radius vector, phi the projected polar angle, i the inclination, Omega the node, Pi a perihelion-type angle. The first line, rho^2 dphi/dt = (left blank), is the areal law. It holds for the projected motion because orthogonal projection multiplies areas by cos i, so rho^2 dphi/dt = h cos i is constant. This is exactly the setting of the apparent orbit of a visual double star (or any orbit seen projected on the sky). It is plausibly that, but the page gives no explicit statement of purpose. The page is unrelated to the neighbouring pages (rigid-body kinetic energy before; continued-fraction recursions after).

(1) POLAR EQUATION OF THE PROJECTED ORBIT. In the orbital plane take coordinates (x, y') with the x-axis along the node line. The reference-plane coordinates are x and y = y' cos i. Write psi = phi - Omega, so x = rho cos psi and y = rho sin psi. Then
 r^2 = x^2 + y^2/cos^2 i = rho^2 (1 - sin^2 i cos^2 psi)/cos^2 i.
The conic is 1/r = 1/p + (e/p) cos(u - omega). Multiplying by r turns the eccentric part into a term linear in x and y', hence linear in x and y. Dividing by rho gives a term of the form beta cos(phi - Pi). [The derivation is mine.] The result is Riemann's
 1/rho = beta cos(phi - Pi) + (1/(p cos i)) sqrt(1 - sin^2 i cos^2(phi - Omega)).
This is correct.

(2) BINET-TYPE EQUATION. Since rho^2 dphi/dt is constant, the projected motion is a central-force motion. Its force law follows from u'' + u with u = 1/rho, differentiating with respect to phi. The term beta cos(phi - Pi) is annihilated by the operator. For f = sqrt(1 - k^2 cos^2 psi) one has f'' + f = (1 - k^2)/f^3 [verified by me]. Hence
 d^2(1/rho)/dphi^2 + 1/rho = c / (1 - sin^2 i cos^2(phi - Omega))^{3/2}, with c = cos i / p.
Riemann writes the right side under an integral sign with limits alpha to pi + alpha. The right side has period pi in phi, so this signals averaging over one period, i.e. a Fourier expansion of the right side in multiples of 2(phi - Omega).

(3) FOURIER COEFFICIENTS VIA A COMPLETE ELLIPTIC INTEGRAL. He writes the 2nd-harmonic coefficient as (c/pi) * Integral_0^pi cos(2phi) dphi / (1 - sin^2 i sin^2 phi)^{3/2}. Here phi has been shifted by pi/2, which only flips the sign of the cos 2 term. He then introduces
 K(m, n) = Integral_0^{pi/2} dphi / sqrt(m^2 cos^2 phi + n^2 sin^2 phi).
With m = 1 and n = cos i this equals the integral of dphi / sqrt(1 - sin^2 i sin^2 phi). Differentiating under the integral sign [step mine]:
 K_m = -m Int cos^2/D^3 and K_n = -n Int sin^2/D^3, where D^2 = m^2 cos^2 + n^2 sin^2.
Hence:
- (1/m)K_m + (1/n)K_n = -Int_0^{pi/2} dphi/D^3. This gives the mean term.
- (1/m)K_m - (1/n)K_n = -Int_0^{pi/2} cos 2phi dphi/D^3. This gives the 2nd harmonic.

Expanding cos 2(phi - Omega) = cos 2phi cos 2Omega + sin 2phi sin 2Omega, the 2nd-harmonic amplitude is multiplied by cos 2Omega and by sin 2Omega. This produces his lines
 ((1/m)K_m - (1/n)K_n) cos 2Omega and (...) sin 2Omega.

(4) EULER'S HOMOGENEITY RELATION. K is homogeneous of degree -1 in (m, n), so m K_m + n K_n = -K. This lets the needed derivatives be reduced to K and one other integral; in modern terms, to K(k) and E(k), since Int dphi/D^3 = E/cos^2 i when m = 1.

In sum, the page reduces the constant and 2nd-harmonic Fourier coefficients of the effective central-force law of a projected Kepler orbit to complete elliptic integrals.
errors: The 2nd-harmonic coefficient is written (c/pi) * Integral_0^pi cos 2phi ...; the standard Fourier coefficient for period pi is (2/pi) * Integral_0^pi. The factor 1/pi is correct for the mean term only. Minor normalization slip, or just shorthand.

The sin 2Omega line appears to read ((1/n) dK/dm - (1/m?) dK/dn). By the cos 2(phi - Omega) expansion it should carry the same factor as the cos 2Omega line, ((1/m)K_m - (1/n)K_n). This is either a slip or a misreading of a hastily written index.

The integral sign with limits alpha to pi+alpha on the right of the Binet equation is not a valid equation as written. It is shorthand for averaging the right-hand side over one period, and the differential is missing.
Switching cos^2(phi - Omega) to sin^2 phi in the Fourier integral is a shift by pi/2, which reverses the sign of the cos 2 coefficient. This is not noted, but it is harmless if tracked.
rho^2 dphi/dt = is left blank; the constant should be h cos i.

results.what: Polar equation of the orthogonal projection of an inclined Kepler conic: 1/rho = beta cos(phi - Pi) + sqrt(1 - sin^2 i cos^2(phi - Omega))/(p cos i)
results.modern_name: apparent (projected) orbit of a visual binary / projected Keplerian ellipse

results.what: Projected motion obeys the areal law and a Binet equation u'' + u = c (1 - sin^2 i cos^2(phi - Omega))^{-3/2}, using f + f'' = (1 - k^2)/f^3
results.modern_name: Binet's equation; apparent central-force law of a projected orbit
results.usually_credited_to: Binet (1810s); the apparent-force observation is classical (Newton, Principia, on projected conics)

results.what: Fourier coefficients of (1 - k^2 sin^2 phi)^{-3/2} expressed via partial derivatives of K(m,n) = Int_0^{pi/2} dphi/sqrt(m^2 cos^2 + n^2 sin^2)
results.modern_name: complete elliptic integrals K, E via differentiation of the homogeneous (Gauss/AGM-type) form
Euler's homogeneous-function theorem applied to the AGM-form elliptic integral

deep.surprise_reason: Routine celestial-mechanics and elliptic-integral computation, a short private calculation. It is mildly interesting as evidence of Riemann working on the projected (apparent) orbit problem, but contains nothing non-standard.

transcription_corrections: 'sin i^2' and 'cos(...)^2' mean sin^2 i and cos^2(...), Riemann's notation.
The integral on the right of the Binet equation has upper limit pi+alpha and lower limit alpha, as transcribed. The integrand numerator is c, and no dphi is written.
The third K-line, (... ) sin 2Omega, is hard to read; the image suggests (1/n dK/dm - 1/n dK/dn) or similar. Mathematically it should be ((1/m)dK/dm - (1/n)dK/dn).
In the last integral the denominator reads sqrt(m^2 cos phi^2 + n^2 sin phi^2), i.e. m^2 cos^2 phi + n^2 sin^2 phi.

The page also has an unlabeled sketch of an ellipse (or circle) with a marked interior point, not at the centre, and two chords through it. This fits the projected orbit with the attracting body not at the centre.
